precepts.text: The king's servants said, Behold, thy servants are ready to do whatsoever my lord the king shall appoint; always ready, whatever is needed.
precepts.point: The boundary stands: if an order breaks the commandments of God, no. But if it falls within the boundaries of the commandments, be willing without hesitation to do what your leader tells you. Whatever position you hold in the body, you are a servant, and when the opportunity comes to fulfill an order you need to be ready; that readiness is the spirit we lack in Israel.

note.label: Joshua 1: The Charge to Joshua and the Formula for Success

precepts.why:
“All that thou commandest us we will do, and whithersoever thou sendest us, we will go.” That is loyalty and the willingness to obey orders, something the Lord loves, and part of the spirit it takes to obtain the promised land. The king's servants had the same spirit: “Behold, thy servants are ready to do whatsoever my lord the king shall appoint.”

Always ready, whatever is needed. The boundary stands: if an order breaks the commandments of God, no. But if it falls within the boundaries of the commandments, be willing without hesitation to do what your leader tells you. Whatever position you hold in the body, you are a servant, and when the opportunity comes to fulfill an order you need to be ready. That readiness is the spirit we lack in Israel.

precepts.text: The counsel of Ahithophel was as if a man had inquired at the oracle of God, so was all his counsel with both David and Absalom.
precepts.point: Ahithophel was such a good counsellor that his counsel was said to be like inquiring at the oracle of God, like talking to an angel of the Most High. So David prayed the Most High would turn that counsel into foolishness, and sent his friend Hushai to act like Absalom's servant so he could listen to Ahithophel's counsel and intervene. This was a game of chess, not checkers, and that is how we have to treat this thing today.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

precepts.why:
“And the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom.”

That is why it mattered when “one told David, saying, Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.” Ahithophel was such a good counsellor that his counsel was like inquiring at the oracle of God, like talking to an angel of the Most High. So David, weeping as he went up mount Olivet, prayed, “O Lord, I pray thee, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”

And he did not stop at praying. He sent his friend Hushai the Archite back to the city to say unto Absalom, “I will be thy servant, O king”, so he could hear Ahithophel’s counsel and intervene: “then mayest thou for me defeat the counsel of Ahithophel.” Everything he heard would go to Zadok and Abiathar the priests and on to David by their two sons. This was a game of chess, not checkers, and that is how we have to treat this thing today.

precepts.text: David sends Hushai back to Absalom to defeat Ahithophel's counsel and to report through Zadok and Abiathar; the name Hushai means loyal to the king.
precepts.point: Absalom and all the men of Israel said Hushai's counsel was better than Ahithophel's. The Lord had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that He might bring evil upon Absalom. The Lord was working with Hushai and David, while Satan was in the spirit of Absalom and Ahithophel.

note.label: 2 Samuel 17: The Counsel of the Lord Shall Stand

precepts.why:
When David came to the top of the mount, Hushai the Archite met him “with his coat rent, and earth upon his head”. David sent him back: “if thou return to the city, and say unto Absalom, I will be thy servant, O king; as I have been thy father’s servant hitherto, so will I now also be thy servant: then mayest thou for me defeat the counsel of Ahithophel.” Whatever he heard out of the king’s house he was to tell Zadok and Abiathar the priests, and send to David by their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan. The name Hushai means loyal to the king.

That is the man Absalom called when he wanted a second opinion: “Call now Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear likewise what he saith.” Hushai was a counterintelligence agent, a spy planted in righteousness, always siding with King David.

So he told Absalom, “The counsel that Ahithophel hath given is not good at this time.” He reminded him that his father and his men were mighty men, “chafed in their minds, as a bear robbed of her whelps in the field”, war ready and strategic, and that David “will not lodge with the people” but moves by night. He warned that if some were overthrown at the first, even he “whose heart is as the heart of a lion, shall utterly melt”, for all Israel knew David was a mighty man. David and his mighty men were on another level; none of Absalom’s thousands could compare to them.

Then he counselled that all Israel be gathered “from Dan even to Beer–sheba, as the sand that is by the sea for multitude”, with Absalom going to battle in his own person. It was deliberately inaccurate counsel that would waste time gathering troops and give David room to escape. Hushai did exactly what David sent him back to do: he defeated the counsel of Ahithophel.

precepts.text: Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel at the gate, promising he would do them justice if he were made judge.
precepts.point: Absalom and all the men of Israel said Hushai's counsel was better than Ahithophel's. The Lord had appointed to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that He might bring evil upon Absalom. The Lord was working with Hushai and David, while Satan was in the spirit of Absalom and Ahithophel.

note.label: 2 Samuel 17: The Counsel of the Lord Shall Stand

precepts.why:
Absalom “prepared him chariots and horses, and fifty men to run before him”, stood beside the way of the gate, and told every man who came to the king for judgment, “See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee.” Then he said, “Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!” So he stole the hearts of the men of Israel at the gate.

That is how Absalom came to be sitting with Ahithophel and Hushai, asking how to take his father. He took the seat himself. But the Lord was not with him: the Lord was working with Hushai and David, while Satan was in the spirit of Absalom and Ahithophel.

precepts.text: Absalom rose up early and stood beside the way of the gate, and when any man came to the king for judgment Absalom flattered him and kissed him, so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
precepts.point: Lord, how are they increased that trouble me, many are they that rise up against me. Put yourself in that position: David's own son was out to get him, and the men who once served the king were being turned against him.

note.label: Psalm 3: But Thou O Lord Art a Shield for Me

precepts.why:
To know how they increased that trouble David, go back to the history: “Absalom prepared him chariots and horses, and fifty men to run before him. And Absalom rose up early, and stood beside the way of the gate: and it was so, that when any man that had a controversy came to the king for judgment, then Absalom called unto him”.

He asked each man, “Of what city art thou?” and told him, “See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee.” Then he said, “Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!” And “when any man came nigh to him to do him obeisance, he put forth his hand, and took him, and kissed him.”

Absalom flattered every man who came to the king for judgment and kissed him, “so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.” That is how the men who once served the king were turned against David, and why he says many are they that rise up against me.

precepts.text: Absalom was making a power play, conspiring to overthrow his father, and the conspiracy was strong for the people increased continually with Absalom, so David told his servants to arise and flee lest Absalom overtake them.
precepts.point: Lord, how are they increased that trouble me, many are they that rise up against me. Put yourself in that position: David's own son was out to get him, and the men who once served the king were being turned against him.

note.label: Psalm 3: But Thou O Lord Art a Shield for Me

precepts.why:
Absalom was making a power play, conspiring to overthrow his father: “And Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counsellor, from his city, even from Giloh, while he offered sacrifices. And the conspiracy was strong; for the people increased continually with Absalom.”

The people increased continually with Absalom; that is “how are they increased that trouble me!” “And there came a messenger to David, saying, The hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom. And David said unto all his servants that were with him at Jerusalem, Arise, and let us flee; for we shall not else escape from Absalom: make speed to depart, lest he overtake us suddenly, and bring evil upon us, and smite the city with the edge of the sword.”

David told his servants to arise and flee lest Absalom overtake them. Read the psalm remembering this heading: David fleeing from his own son. If you do not know that history, go back to Second Samuel and read it, and put yourself in the scriptures to better your understanding.

precepts.text: Ahithophel, King David's own counselor, left him and joined Absalom's conspiracy to steal the kingdom, and that is betrayal.
precepts.point: This is betrayal by someone you know well. Some have suffered these things in the past, and some have suffered them in the truth.

note.label: Psalm 55: Cast Thy Burden Upon the Lord

precepts.why:
“For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it”. It was a man his equal, his guide and his acquaintance. That is Ahithophel: “Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counsellor, from his city, even from Giloh, while he offered sacrifices. And the conspiracy was strong”. King David's own counsellor left him and joined Absalom's conspiracy to steal the kingdom. “And one told David, saying, Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom. And David said, O Lord, I pray thee, turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness.”

That is betrayal, by someone he took sweet counsel with and walked with to the house of God. Betrayal by someone you know well cuts where an enemy's reproach could not. Some have suffered these things in the past, and some have suffered them in the truth.

points: Absalom prepared chariots and horses and fifty men to run before him, rose up early, and stood beside the way of the gate. When any man came to the king for judgment, Absalom called him, said his matters were good and right but there was no man deputed of the king to hear him, and wished that he himself were made judge in the land that he might do every man justice.

This is the sneakiness Absalom did: he began to underhand the king, winning the love of the people behind the king's back, so that he could later betray him, as the prophecy said the sword would not depart from David's house.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

points: When any man came near to do him obeisance, Absalom put forth his hand, took him, and kissed him, and on this manner he did to all Israel that came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.

Instead of going to the king and resolving things, Absalom got into the king's good graces, then went around patting people on the back and stroking them. This is what the bishop calls friendish, showing people friendship without being a true friend.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

points: This shows the simplicity of a lot of brothers in Israel: a man who says all the nice things and gains favor in your eyes goes completely against leadership and out of order, and you follow along carnally, not spiritually, because he kissed your hand and told you everything would be all right.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

points: After forty years Absalom asked leave to go pay his vow in Hebron, and the king said, Go in peace. But Absalom sent spies through all the tribes to say, at the sound of the trumpet, Absalom reigneth in Hebron. Two hundred men went with him from Jerusalem in their simplicity, knowing nothing. Absalom also sent for Ahithophel, David's counsellor, and the conspiracy was strong, for the people increased continually with Absalom.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

points: David, being the man of war that he is, saw everyone starting to follow Absalom, and instead of sitting there like a dummy, chose to leave and strategize while he was out.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

points: A messenger told David the hearts of the men of Israel were with Absalom, and David told his servants to arise and flee, lest Absalom overtake them suddenly and smite the city with the sword. The king went forth with all his household, leaving ten women who were concubines to keep the house, and all his servants and the Cherethites, Pelethites, and six hundred Gittites passed on before him.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

points: Ittai showed a level of loyalty that David respected, so David let him come. This loyalty in the face of trouble is the same thing seen throughout Israel's story.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

points: The king told Ittai the Gittite to return, since he was a stranger and an exile who had only just come, and wished him mercy and truth. But Ittai swore that in whatever place the king was, in death or life, there also would his servant be, so David said, Go and pass over, and Ittai passed over with all his men and little ones. All the country wept as the people passed over the brook Kidron toward the wilderness.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

points: Zadok and all the Levites bare the ark of the covenant, and David told Zadok to carry it back into the city, saying if he found favour in the eyes of the Most High, he would be brought again to see it and its habitation; but if not, let the Most High do as seemed good. He also told Zadok the seer to return with his son Ahimaaz and Jonathan the son of Abiathar, and to send him word. So they carried the ark again to Jerusalem.

David sent the ark back in faith: make sure it stays in the city, and if it is the Most High's will, I will return. That is how much faith David had. Many of the songs in the book of Psalms were written while David was on the run like this, and some of it is prophecy of Christ, because the spirit of Christ was in every prophet.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

points: David went up the ascent of Mount Olivet weeping, barefoot, his head covered, and all the people with him weeping. When told that Ahithophel was among the conspirators, David prayed that the Most High turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness. Then Hushai the Archite met him with his coat rent, and David sent him back to the city to feign service to Absalom and defeat Ahithophel's counsel, reporting all he heard to Zadok and Abiathar by their two sons.

note.label: 2 Samuel 15: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel

points: Ahithophel was such a good counsellor that his counsel was said to be like inquiring at the oracle of God, like talking to an angel of the Most High. So David prayed the Most High would turn that counsel into foolishness, and sent his friend Hushai to act like Absalom's servant so he could listen to Ahithophel's counsel and intervene. This was a game of chess, not checkers, and that is how we have to treat this thing today.
